title: TASS vs. Endophthalmitis: A Critical Ophthalmic Showdown
summary: Acute postoperative intraocular inflammation can rapidly threaten vision. Differentiating between sterile Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) and infectious Endophthalmitis is paramount for optimal patient outcomes, as these conditions demand distinct diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. This guide meticulously compares their clinical profiles, etiologies, and management strategies.

rows: Nature
Acute, severe, sterile intraocular inflammatory reaction following anterior segment surgery.
Acute or chronic intraocular infection involving the vitreous cavity and/or anterior chamber.
Etiology
Non-infectious: Toxic irritation from substances entering the anterior chamber during surgery.
Infectious: Microbial invasion (bacterial, fungal) into the eye, often post-surgical.
Key Differentiator
Absence of vitreous involvement (vitritis).
Presence of vitreous involvement (vitritis) is hallmark.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology
content: **TASS:** Incidence is variable, estimated between 0.01% and 0.2% post-cataract surgery. Often occurs in clusters linked to specific surgical batches, equipment, or sterilization protocols. Not linked to specific patient risk factors directly.
**Endophthalmitis:** Incidence typically 0.03% to 0.1% after cataract surgery. Rates vary by region and prophylactic strategies (e.g., intracameral antibiotics).

**Risk Factors for Endophthalmitis:** Posterior capsular rupture, vitreous loss, prolonged surgery, wound dehiscence, use of clear corneal incisions, diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, blepharitis, use of non-preserved balanced salt solution (BSS).

sub: Preservatives (e.g., benzalkonium chloride in topical drops)
Endotoxins (from gram-negative bacteria on reusable instruments)
Ophthalmic Viscosurgical Devices (OVDs) - residues, pH, osmolality
Acute (most common, onset <6 weeks, typically 2-7 days)
Chronic (onset >6 weeks, often indolent, P. acnes, fungal)

rows: Onset
Very early (12-48 hours post-op), sudden
Later (2-7 days post-op for acute bacterial; weeks/months for chronic)
Pain
Mild to moderate, often discomfort, not excruciating
Moderate to severe, deep ocular pain, headache, photophobia
Vision
Decreased, often foggy, but can improve rapidly with treatment
Markedly decreased, often rapidly progressive, profound vision loss
Redness
Diffuse conjunctival injection, often mild
Marked conjunctival injection, chemosis, lid edema
Corneal Edema
Diffuse, limbus-to-limbus, often severe, Descemet's folds
Can be focal or diffuse, often secondary to severe inflammation, may be localized
AC Reaction
Marked cells (WBCs), severe flare, fibrinous membrane, often white fluffy hypopyon
Marked cells, dense flare, fibrin, often creamy/layered hypopyon
Hypopyon
Typically sterile, non-infectious, white/fluffy, often uniform level
Often creamy, layered, containing infectious organisms
IOP
Often elevated due to trabeculitis and blocked outflow
Variable, can be high (inflammation) or low (ciliary body shutdown)
Vitritis
**ABSENT** (unless pre-existing or severe fibrin mimicking)
**PRESENT** (the hallmark sign), often dense ('headlights in fog')
Red Reflex
Often present, though obscured by corneal edema/AC reaction
Often absent due to dense vitritis
Pupil
Often dilated/fixed due to iris sphincter damage, pigment dispersion
Miotic, irregular, or fixed from inflammation and posterior synechiae
Lids/Conjunctiva
Mild swelling, diffuse injection
Marked lid edema, chemosis, severe injection
Cornea
Diffuse limbus-to-limbus edema, Descemet's folds, few KPs
Variable edema (focal or diffuse), endothelial plaques, numerous KPs
Anterior Chamber
3-4+ cells & flare, often dense fibrin, white fluffy hypopyon, iris atrophy, pigment dispersion
3-4+ cells & flare, dense fibrin, creamy/layered hypopyon, posterior synechiae
Iris
Poor pupillary dilation, sphincter damage, iris atrophy, possibly transillumination defects
Synechiae (posterior, anterior), possibly rubeosis, necrosis, heterochromia
Lens/IOL
IOL often clean or with fine deposits; capsule usually intact
IOL covered in inflammatory material; capsule potentially compromised, often with plaque
Vitreous
Clear (unless pre-existing pathology or severe fibrin can mimic)
Dense vitritis, often obscures fundus view ('headlights in fog'), vitreous opacities/abscesses
Fundus
Normal view (once corneal/AC clear); optic disc and macula usually unaffected directly
Obscured or absent view, retinal infiltrates, vasculitis, hemorrhages, periphlebitis, edema
Gonioscopy
Wide-open angle (unless pre-existing), trabeculitis signs, possibly pigment
Synechial angle closure, inflammatory debris in angle, possibly neovascularization

sections.title: 7. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **1. Clinical Assessment & History:** Thorough history, surgical details, symptom onset, progression.

**2. Ocular Examination:** Detailed slit-lamp exam, dilated fundus exam, IOP measurement, B-scan ultrasonography (essential if fundus view obscured, to rule out retinal detachment/vitreous abscesses).
**3. Anterior Chamber (AC) Tap (Paracentesis):** Collect 0.1-0.2 mL of aqueous fluid. Send for:
• Gram stain (rapid preliminary result, low sensitivity)
• Cultures (aerobic, anaerobic, fungal – on blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud's dextrose agar)
• PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) for bacterial/fungal DNA (high sensitivity/specificity, rapid results for common pathogens).
• Cytology (if TASS suspected, to rule out infectious organisms and identify inflammatory cells).

**4. Vitreous Tap (Vitreous Biopsy):** Performed if AC tap is inconclusive or vitritis is dense. Collect 0.1-0.5 mL of undiluted vitreous. (Higher yield for culture than AC tap). Same lab tests as AC tap.

**5. Systemic Workup (for Endogenous Endophthalmitis):** Blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP, urine culture, chest X-ray, echocardiogram, referral to internal medicine/infectious disease if systemic source suspected.

rows: Postoperative Uveitis (Non-infectious)
Less severe, gradual onset, usually responds well to topical steroids; typically NO vitritis; milder AC reaction.
Retained Lens Fragments
Can cause chronic inflammation (often granulomatous), usually a history of complicated surgery, visible fragments on exam/US; may not have dense vitritis initially.
Sympathetic Ophthalmia
Bilateral granulomatous uveitis, history of penetrating trauma or intraocular surgery to one eye (2 weeks to years later); 'Dalén-Fuchs nodules'.
Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN)
Severe vitritis, anterior uveitis, widespread necrotizing retinitis (often peripheral), occlusive vasculopathy. Viral etiology (HSV, VZV). Fundus involvement is primary.
Phacolytic Glaucoma
High IOP, mature/hypermature cataract, visible lens material/macrophages in AC, ruptured lens capsule. Inflammation secondary to lens protein leakage.
Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage
Acute severe pain, rock-hard eye, shallow AC, fundus view obscured by hemorrhage. Usually intraoperative or immediate post-op. B-scan shows choroidal elevation.
Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB)
History of trauma, visible IOFB, localized inflammation. Signs of siderosis/chalcosis if metallic.
Pre-existing Uveitis Exacerbation
History of uveitis, often milder flare-up, responds to usual uveitis treatment.

sections.title: 9. Staging / Grading
sections.content: Neither TASS nor Endophthalmitis have formal staging systems. Severity is generally assessed by initial visual acuity, density of AC reaction and vitritis, and extent of fibrin formation. The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) uses initial visual acuity to stratify prognosis for acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis, specifically noting outcomes for patients presenting with light perception (LP) only vs. hand motions (HM) or better.

sections.title: 10. Management & Treatment Algorithm
content: **STEP 1: Immediate Triage & Differentiation:** Based on clinical features (especially onset, pain, and presence/absence of vitritis). If doubt exists, treat as Endophthalmitis.
**STEP 2: TASS Management (Presumed Sterile):**
• **Topical Corticosteroids:** High-dose, frequent (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h or Dexamethasone 0.1% q1h). Taper rapidly as inflammation subsides.
• **Cycloplegics:** (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% bid-tid, Atropine 1% bid) to reduce pain and prevent posterior synechiae.
• **IOP Management:** If elevated, topical anti-glaucoma medications (e.g., topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors).
• **Systemic Steroids:** Reserved for severe, recalcitrant cases (e.g., oral Prednisone 40-60mg/day, tapered).
• **Anterior Chamber Wash:** If severe fibrin, hypopyon, or persistently high IOP (therapeutic and diagnostic by removing toxic substances).
**STEP 3: Endophthalmitis Management (Presumed Infectious):**
• **A. Obtain Samples:** Perform AC and/or vitreous tap for Gram stain, cultures, and PCR (as per 'Investigations' section).
• **B. Intravitreal Antibiotics:** IMMEDIATELY after samples are taken. Empirical broad-spectrum coverage:
• Vancomycin (Gram-positive): 1.0 mg in 0.1 mL.
• Ceftazidime (Gram-negative): 2.25 mg in 0.1 mL.
• OR Amikacin (if severe penicillin allergy or suspected atypical Gram-negatives): 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (use with caution due to retinal toxicity).
• **C. Intravitreal Dexamethasone:** 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (controversial, typically given concurrent with antibiotics to reduce inflammation, but potential to mask infection).

• **D. Systemic Antibiotics:** Oral Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Moxifloxacin 400mg PO daily) or IV antibiotics may be considered, but intravitreal agents are primary due to poor blood-retina barrier penetration.

• **E. Topical Medications:** Topical fortified antibiotics (e.g., Vancomycin 50mg/mL, Ceftazidime 100mg/mL) and topical corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% q1h) to control surface inflammation.
• **F. Vitrectomy:** Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) is indicated for:
• Patients presenting with initial visual acuity of Light Perception (LP) or worse (EVS criteria).
• Cases with dense vitritis, retinal detachment, or non-resolving infection/abscesses.
• Fungal endophthalmitis (often requires vitrectomy and intravitreal antifungals like Amphotericin B 0.005-0.01mg/0.1mL or Voriconazole 0.1mg/0.1mL).

sections.title: 11. Surgical Techniques: Vitrectomy
content: **1. Pre-op:** Topical povidone-iodine, peribulbar/retrobulbar anesthesia, sterile field.
**2. Incisions:** Typically 23, 25, or 27-gauge pars plana vitrectomy. Sclerotomies placed 3-4 mm posterior to the limbus (depending on phakic/aphakic status).
**3. Vitreous Sample:** Collect initial vitreous for cultures/PCR.
**4. Core Vitrectomy:** Remove as much infected vitreous gel as possible to reduce microbial load and inflammatory mediators. Use high cut rates and low aspiration.
**5. Peripheral Vitrectomy:** Careful removal of peripheral vitreous (may require scleral depression).
**6. Inspection:** Inspect retina for infiltrates, detachment, tears.
**7. Intravitreal Injections:** Administer intravitreal antibiotics (Vancomycin, Ceftazidime) and often dexamethasone at the end of the procedure.
**8. Closure:** Sclerotomy sites are hydrated or sutured as needed. Topical antibiotics.

sections.title: 12. Complications & Prognosis
content: **TASS:**
• Permanent corneal decompensation/edema (bullous keratopathy).
• Secondary glaucoma (due to trabeculitis, pigment dispersion).
• Iris atrophy, pupillary distortion/fixation, pigment dispersion glaucoma.
• Cystoid macular edema (CME).
• Prognosis generally good with prompt, appropriate treatment. Visual recovery often excellent.
**Endophthalmitis:**
• Permanent severe vision loss, blindness.
• Retinal detachment.
• Hypotony, phthisis bulbi (end-stage eye with severe shrinkage).
• Secondary glaucoma.
• Corneal decompensation/scarring.
• Choroidal detachment, suprachoroidal hemorrhage.

• Prognosis is guarded, dependent on organism virulence, initial visual acuity, and rapidity of treatment. Staphylococcal infections generally have better outcomes than Streptococcal or Gram-negative.

• EVS showed 53% of patients with VA of LP or worse achieved 20/40 or better with vitrectomy + antibiotics; 33% of patients with VA HM or better achieved 20/40 or better with tap/biopsy + antibiotics.

sections.title: 13. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Severe, rapidly worsening ocular pain and profound vision loss post-op.**
**Any evidence of vitreous inflammation (vitritis) on dilated fundus exam or B-scan.**
**Absent red reflex.**
**Creamy, layered hypopyon.**
**Unilateral and progressively severe inflammation.**
**Any doubt regarding diagnosis: Treat aggressively as Endophthalmitis until proven otherwise. Delay is vision lost.**
**Failure of inflammation to respond to high-dose topical steroids within 24-48 hours.**

content.mnemonic: TASS vs. ENDO: 3 P's and V

sections.title: 15. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **Vitritis is THE critical differentiating factor.** If you see vitritis, it's endophthalmitis until proven otherwise.
**Timing of onset is crucial:** TASS typically 12-48 hours, Endophthalmitis 2-7 days (acute).
**Corneal Edema:** Limbus-to-limbus edema suggests TASS; focal/patchy edema is less specific but can be seen in endophthalmitis.
**Hypopyon:** TASS hypopyon is often uniform, white, and 'fluffy'; endophthalmitis hypopyon can be layered, creamy, and denser.
**IOP:** Often high in TASS due to trabeculitis; variable in endophthalmitis (high from inflammation, low from ciliary body shutdown).
**Clusters of cases strongly suggest TASS,** indicating a breach in sterilization or surgical material contamination.
**Never delay treatment for endophthalmitis to await culture results.** Treat empirically with broad-spectrum intravitreal antibiotics immediately after obtaining samples.
**Intracameral antibiotics (e.g., cefuroxime 1mg/0.1mL) at the end of cataract surgery have significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative endophthalmitis.**

sections.title: 16. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content:
The **Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS)** (1995) remains the cornerstone for management of acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis. It demonstrated the benefit of immediate vitrectomy for patients with initial visual acuity of light perception or worse, compared to tap/biopsy alone. For those with better vision, tap/biopsy with intravitreal antibiotics yielded similar results to vitrectomy. 

Recent advances include the widespread adoption of **intracameral antibiotics** (e.g., cefuroxime, moxifloxacin) for prophylaxis, significantly reducing post-cataract endophthalmitis rates. **PCR-based diagnostics** offer faster and more sensitive identification of causative organisms, even with small sample sizes, guiding targeted antibiotic therapy sooner.

sections.title: 17. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
sections.content:
**Pediatric Patients:** Diagnosis can be challenging in non-verbal children. Signs like irritability, eyelid swelling, and extreme photophobia may be more prominent. Pediatric eyes may have a more robust inflammatory response, potentially leading to faster disease progression and more severe complications like amblyopia. High index of suspicion is crucial.

**Immunocompromised Patients:** (e.g., HIV/AIDS, diabetics, organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressants) are at higher risk for opportunistic infections and more virulent courses of endophthalmitis. Fungal or atypical bacterial infections should be considered more readily. Systemic workup for endogenous sources is particularly important in this group.
